To assemble a sample, RiboPilot compares its reads to known ribosomal sequences
from related organisms. It comes ready to use for **ray-finned fishes**. For any
other group, you build that reference data once, and it is reused for every future
project on that group.

You do not need to find or format any sequences yourself, and in most projects you
do not need to run a command by hand either: the app's **Reference tab** does this
for you, using the taxonomy you have already assigned. This guide covers that tab
first, then the console commands underneath it, for anyone who wants to build a
database ahead of time or from a script.

# The Reference tab

The Reference tab sits between the **Taxonomy** and **Assemble** tabs. Until a
group has a database of its own, its samples are assembled against RiboPilot's
built-in **ray-finned fish** reference, which is usually the wrong choice outside
fish. This tab is where you replace it.

Once your samples' taxonomy is assigned, open the tab and press **Propose
groups**. RiboPilot looks at each sample's lineage and groups samples that can
share one reference database, using how many ribosomal sequences GenBank already
holds for each candidate group: a group needs at least 1,000 GenBank records to
make a useful reference, and RiboPilot picks the narrowest group (family, order,
class, and so on) that clears that bar, without letting it grow past about 25,000
records. Samples from very different parts of the tree end up in different
groups, each getting its own database.

Each row is one proposed group. The **Status** column says where that group
stands ("Needs a database", "Building", "Ready", "Build failed", or "Left on
current database"), and the rest of the row shows the clade, how many of your
samples it covers, and how many GenBank records back it up.

## Setting a group up

The link at the right-hand end of each row says what that group needs: **Set up
database**, **Try again**, or **Change**. Click it and you are offered four
choices:

- **Download sequences from GenBank.** The normal choice. Opens a run window, the
  same kind the Assemble tab uses, showing the command that will run and letting
  you set an NCBI API key or restrict to RefSeq records first. Press Run and the
  download happens through RiboPilot's Nextflow workflow, with a live progress
  board and Stop / Close controls; you can keep working in the app while it runs.
  If you are using RiboPilot through a remote browser, the window instead offers
  an editable cluster job script to submit or save. When a build finishes,
  RiboPilot automatically points that group's samples at the new database and
  writes the files to your reference folder (see below). Samples already locked
  in the Assemble tab are left alone, since their results were produced with
  whatever database they had before. A group whose database already exists on
  disk is wired up immediately, without starting a new build.
- **Use a database I already have.** Points the group at a database that was
  already built, either earlier in this project or by someone else sharing the
  same reference folder.
- **Change which clade this group uses.** Opens the group's shared lineage as a
  ladder, from the broadest rank down to the narrowest, each rung showing how
  many samples it covers and, for rungs RiboPilot has already counted, how many
  GenBank records back them up; an uncounted rung shows "records unknown" rather
  than triggering a new count. Pick a different rung to widen or narrow the
  group, or search for another clade entirely. If the rung you pick does not
  cover every sample in the group, the leftover samples are split off into a
  group of their own so nobody is left under the wrong reference. You can also
  reach this by clicking the group's **Clade** cell directly.
- **Leave these samples on the built-in fish database.** Nothing is built. Only
  sensible if your samples really are ray-finned fishes, or if you have already
  pointed their assembly settings at some other database yourself.

To handle several groups at once, tick their rows first, then click the link on
any one of them: the choice you make applies to the whole selection. The clade
option is offered only for a single group, since the ladder walks one group's
shared lineage.

Working through the Reference tab is optional. If you start the Assemble step
with groups that are still unresolved, RiboPilot warns you but goes ahead: those
samples simply assemble with whatever database their assembly settings already
have, same as if you had left them on the fish database.

# The reference folder

Built databases live in a **reference folder** that is shared across projects: one
clade database, built once, is reused by every project that needs that clade, and
if the folder is on a shared drive, by everyone in your lab. You can set it in the
Reference tab with the **Settings** button (which also lets you adjust the minimum
and maximum record counts the grouping step uses), or when you create a project:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path       = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads",
  executor   = "conda",
  ref_dir    = "~/ribopilot_refs"
)
```

If you do not set a folder, RiboPilot uses a default location on your computer.

<div class="alert alert-note">
The <code>executor = "conda"</code> shown in the examples on this page is
<strong>no longer a supported way to run</strong>. Supported execution is Docker or Singularity; use
<code>executor = "docker"</code> on a workstation, and see the
<a href="RiboPilot.html">Get started guide</a> for clusters. The examples keep
<code>"conda"</code> only so they match the rest of the documentation.
</div>

# Building from the console

You can also build a reference database directly, without going through the app,
using `build_reference_db()`. This is useful for building a database ahead of
time, from a script, or on a machine without a browser; the app itself builds
databases through its own Nextflow workflow and does not call this function.
It takes a standard NCBI
search (the same kind of query you would type on the
[NCBI website](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/)) and a short label for the group. It
then downloads the relevant 18S, 5.8S, 28S, and ITS sequences and prepares the
reference data.

```{r, purl = FALSE}
# 1. First, just check how many sequences are available. Nothing is downloaded.
RiboPilot::build_reference_db(
  '"Gastropoda"[Organism]', "gastropoda",
  count_only = TRUE, conda_env = "ribopilot"
)

# 2. Then build the reference data and save it somewhere you can reuse.
db <- RiboPilot::build_reference_db(
  '"Gastropoda"[Organism]', "gastropoda",
  out_dir = "~/ribopilot_refs", conda_env = "ribopilot"
)
```

Replace `Gastropoda` with your group. The `"[Organism]"` part tells NCBI to search
by organism name, so `'"Gastropoda"[Organism]'` means "all gastropod sequences".
The second value, `"gastropoda"`, is just a short label used in the file names.

<div class="alert alert-note">
Running this needs the tools you installed with conda, so start R from a terminal
where you have run <code>conda activate ribopilot</code>, or keep the
<code>conda_env = "ribopilot"</code> setting shown above. That is the unsupported
local-tools path: building from the app's Reference tab instead runs the same work
inside the container, which is the supported route.
</div>

To use a database built this way in a project, point the project at it by adding
two lines to `new_project()`:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path       = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads",
  executor   = "conda",
  custom_seeds_db  = db$seeds,
  custom_labels_db = db$labels
)
```

# Good to know

- **Build once, reuse forever.** If you run `build_reference_db()` again for the
  same group and location, it reuses what you already built instead of
  re-downloading; add `overwrite = TRUE` to force a fresh rebuild. From the
  Reference tab, a group whose database already exists on disk is simply
  wired up without starting a new build.
- **Groups with few sequences.** Some groups have very little published ribosomal
  data. If your search returns only a handful of records (check with
  `count_only = TRUE` first), broaden it to a larger group. For example, search a
  whole family or order rather than a single genus, so RiboPilot has enough
  reference sequence to work with. The Reference tab does this automatically by
  walking up the lineage until it finds a clade with enough records.
- **The 5.8S gene.** GenBank rarely stores 5.8S on its own; it is usually bundled
  inside ITS records. That is fine: RiboPilot still recovers the 5.8S region from
  the full repeat, and its quality checks anchor on the 18S and 28S genes.
